title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) loop affects verifier-detected safety violations for LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 intent→configuration tasks stratified across VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change clusters) we compared: (1) baseline — a single LLM proposal produced once per task, and (2) guarded — the identical shared LLM proposal validated by a deterministic netops verifier and subjected to up to one automated repair iteration if the verifier flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002; paired-bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). The preregistered exact McNemar two-sided test was implemented as an exact binomial on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01); with n = 1 and n10 = 1 the archived two-sided p = 1.00 under that convention. Interpretation: on this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; measured marginal verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric is therefore small, though the verifier corrected at least one concrete baseline failure. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are rapidly being applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and programmatic repair. System reports and surveys emphasize that operational safety depends heavily on surrounding engineering: deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback mechanisms [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. A recurrent operational pattern is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): an LLM generates a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks a set of formalized properties, and automated or human-in-the-loop repairs are applied for violations. Despite conceptual consensus, controlled measurements that isolate the marginal contribution of a verifier (holding the model’s proposal fixed) are scarce. Practitioners need to know: when an LLM already produces high-quality candidates (on verifier-modeled properties), how much incremental safety does a verifier plus a modest automated repair budget provide on a verifier-scoped pass/fail metric? We answer this narrow operational question via a preregistered paired experiment that isolates verifier+repair impact under canonical, deterministic semantics.
sections.related_work: Deterministic and formal verification approaches (header-space analysis, route-model verifiers, Batfish-style analyzers) provide machine-checkable network properties (reachability, isolation, update atomicity) and underpin verifier-in-the-loop designs [Beckett et al., 2017]. Recent NetOps/AIOps research explores LLM-based intent translation and agentic frameworks that advocate guardrails and validators (e.g., INTA, Confucius, other agentic NetOps systems) [INTA, 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–verify–repair or generate–critic patterns are proposed across structured-generation domains to reduce unsafe outputs [PoeTone; INTA]. Separate literature documents failure modes of LLM-driven automation (hallucination, overconfidence, tool-integration errors) and recommends verification or human oversight as mitigations [Owen, 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2025]. However, the supplied evidence set lacks a controlled, preregistered ablation that quantitatively isolates the verifier’s marginal contribution for identical LLM proposals; our study provides such an artifact-backed measurement.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The study was preregistered (study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026) and froze the research question, inclusion/exclusion rules, deterministic task seeds, estimands, analysis executor, multiplicity plan, retry policy, and stopping rule. Confirmatory hypothesis H1: an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration will produce a lower verifier-detected safety-violation rate than the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback (paired within-task). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations.

Task generation and strata. A deterministic synthetic corpus of 500 intent→configuration tasks was generated with deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and preregistered seeds. The preregistered stratification and the executed allocation were VLAN-change: 167 tasks; ACL-change: 167 tasks; static-route-change: 166 tasks. No confirmatory exclusions occurred and the deterministic_reconciliation manifest confirms complete_pair_count = 500 and failed_episode_count = 0.

Generation semantics and adapters. To isolate verifier effect we used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (independent_condition_generation = false). For each task the pipeline produced a single shared LLM proposal; that identical candidate served as the baseline output and was also validated by the guarded arm. The guarded arm invoked the single automated repair call only if the deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) reported a preregistered high/medium-severity violation on the shared candidate. Requested LLM = gpt-5-mini via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; model parameters and provider are archived in execution/model_configuration.json.

Primary statistical test and exact implementation. The preregistered confirmatory test was an exact McNemar two-sided test on paired binary outcomes. The archived analysis executor implemented the test as an exact binomial on discordant pairs: let n = n10 + n01 (discordant pairs), and let k = n10 (pairs where guarded passes and baseline fails under the executor’s discordant-ordering convention). The two-sided p-value is computed from X ∼ Binomial(n, 0.5) as p_two-sided = 2 × min{P(X ≤ k), P(X ≥ k)} truncated at 1.0 (equivalently: p_two-sided = 2 × min{BinomCDF(n,k), 1 − BinomCDF(n,k−1)} with truncation to 1.0). This exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and its code-path are archived in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. We report the archived p computed under that convention.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes. The run completed with complete_pair_count = 500 and model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair-stage calls observed = 1). Aggregated per-condition counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv) are: baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). The paired contingency table (guarded × baseline; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002.

Inference and uncertainty. Applying the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs computation with n = 1 and k = 1 yields two-sided p = 1.00 (executor convention). Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute difference (B = 10,000, seed = 1729; resampling preserved pairing) is [0.0, 0.006]. These analysis outputs and the exact bootstrap parameters are archived in analysis/* artifacts.

Repair activity and discordant episode provenance. Observed repair-stage calls = 1; that single repair produced the sole discordant outcome (n10 = 1): the guarded arm converted one baseline-detected preregistered high/medium-severity violation into a verified pass. The execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation confirm precisely one repair-stage invocation and one discordant pair. The full per-task validator diagnostics, normalized configurations, repair prompt and repair response, and provider-call traces for that episode are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl and provider_call traces; the manifest records the hash for execution/raw_results.jsonl. Deterministic retrieval procedure: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for entries with baseline verifier pass == 0 and guarded verifier pass == 1; because only one such entry exists in the confirmatory set this deterministically returns the single discordant pair and its archived validator_trace and repair-provider trace. The archived validator_trace shows the baseline failure class as a preregistered high/medium-severity violation and the archived repair response produced a modified configuration that the validator then marked valid (zero high/medium-severity violations). The manifest and per-task archives provide the concrete repair prompt/response content for audit; we avoid reproducing provider-sensitive raw call content in the paper body and instead provide the deterministic retrieval method and archive reference paths.
sections.discussion:
Operational interpretation. Under the constrained experimental regime—single requested LLM (gpt-5-mini), shared_initial_candidate semantics, a deterministic verifier modeling a limited feature set (allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}), and at most one automated repair iteration—the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals and the marginal measured pass-rate benefit of adding the verifier was small (0.002). This is a conditional result: it documents that when baseline proposal quality (on verifier-scoped properties) is very high, measurable pass-rate gains from modest verifier+repair budgets may be negligible on a composite pass/fail metric. Still, the verifier demonstrated corrective utility in a concrete case by converting a baseline failure into a pass.

Design-choice implications. The shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolates verifier+repair effect conditional on identical proposals and suits deployment policies that preserve the original proposal for human review. Alternative operational choices—verifier-guided regeneration, multiple repair iterations, or different budget trade-offs—may yield larger effect sizes and require their own preregistration and controlled measurement.

Threats to validity and constructive limitations. Internal validity is supported by preregistration, deterministic seeds, and automated replacement rules; there were no manual adjudications. Construct validity is limited by the verifier’s modeled property set and severity mapping (archived in the validator-spec): measured pass == no high/medium-severity violations is relative to that coverage. External validity is limited by a single model request, a synthetic task corpus, and constrained feature scope; broader cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity and dynamic protocol states are outside the verifier’s modeled domain. Statistically, observed baseline failure prevalence (1/500) created a ceiling effect that reduced sensitivity to detect small absolute improvements; the archived exact McNemar p = 1.00 reflects the executor’s small-n exact-binomial convention and the observed discordant counts.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) isolating the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Baseline proposals passed the deterministic verifier in 499/500 tasks; adding verifier+repair produced 500/500 passes, an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.006]) and an archived exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.00 under the executor’s exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention. The conditional lesson is that when baseline proposal quality is very high for verifier-modeled properties and the verifier coverage is narrow, a modest verifier+repair budget may produce only marginal measured gains on a composite pass/fail metric, although rare concrete failures can still be corrected. We recommend practitioners measure baseline error prevalence on representative workloads, align verifier coverage to operator-critical properties, and select generation/repair semantics consistent with deployment priorities. All preregistration, code, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call logs, and analysis artifacts required to deterministically reproduce and audit these claims are archived in the study evidence bundle.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; task payloads constrained to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single requested model family (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — no claim of multi-model or cross-validator generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the small discordant count.

The single discordant episode (the sole task where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl in the evidence bundle. To inspect it deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair entries where the baseline scoring outcome indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while the guarded scoring outcome indicates pass == 1; because only one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, this lookup returns the single episode and its provider-call traces. The validator violation-code→severity mapping is archived in the execution manifest and validator-spec artifacts in the bundle.
